summary:
Bayelsa State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. It criminalises all forms of same-sex unions and renders any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void. Same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across Nigeria since 1916.

The maximum penalty a visitor faces in Bayelsa is 14 years' imprisonment. That is the ceiling in the southern portion of the country, which includes Bayelsa, and it covers same-sex sexual activity and same-sex unions alike under the 2014 statute.

The death penalty does not reach Bayelsa. It is confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where penalties for same-sex conduct run from lashes or caning up to death by stoning; those provisions have no application in Bayelsa, which stands under the secular national 14-year framework.

The framework governing Bayelsa recognises no gender identity, provides no anti-discrimination protections and recognises no same-sex relationships. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation in the state, and any union they enter is void under the 2014 Act.

No state-specific enforcement divergence is documented for Bayelsa. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people across all states, including the 2014 statute's reach, without identifying any Bayelsa-specific arrest, prosecution or incident.
tangentialFactors:
Bayelsa's exposure is materially narrower than that of the northern Shari'a states. Foreign travel guidance warning of death-penalty risk attaches only to those twelve states, and a visitor in Bayelsa faces the secular 14-year maximum rather than corporal or capital punishment.

The comparison runs the other way as well: the 14-year ceiling in Bayelsa is the highest penalty available in the south, and the 2014 Act's ban on cohabitation, public show of an amorous relationship and operation of gay organisations reaches conduct that would not otherwise be criminal.

The available sources describe Nigeria-wide patterns of arrest, detention and mob violence without a state-level breakdown. Bayelsa does not appear in the inventory as a site of documented enforcement, which reflects the absence of reporting rather than a finding of non-enforcement.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bayelsa face the same 14-year maximum as visitors, with no state-level mitigation, exemption or protective statute recorded in the sources.

No legal recognition of gender identity is available in Bayelsa, and the state records no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation in employment, services or public life.

Same-sex relationships carry no legal recognition in the state; any marriage or civil union between persons of the same sex is invalid and void under the 2014 Act, and the Act's prohibitions on cohabitation and public display apply to residents as they do to visitors.

Bayelsa stands under the secular national criminal code rather than a Shari'a penal code, so residents are not exposed to the lashes, caning or stoning provisions in force elsewhere in the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Bayelsa police have used the 2014 Act against gender presentation, cross-dressing, or possession of binders and other trans-specific items is unresolved: the inventory contains no Bayelsa-specific enforcement record either way.

No Bayelsa-specific incident data on violence against trans people, including killings, assaults or mob action, appears in the sources. The trans-specific killings and police misgendering documented in the national material are not located in Bayelsa, and their absence here is not sourced as evidence of safety.

Whether Bayelsa State has enacted any implementing, aggravating or protective legislation of its own is not sourced. The sources record no state-specific enforcement divergence, but they do not affirmatively establish that none exists.

Access to gender-affirming care, HIV services and post-exposure care within Bayelsa is not documented at state level; the national finding that arrest and extortion risk chills care-seeking has not been tested against Bayelsa facilities.
